neighbours.label: a subject pronoun (he, she, I) opening the next narrative action right after a line of dialogue in fiction
fire: “You came back,” she whispered, and he nodded slowly before taking her hand.
“That’s not fair!” Mia shouted across the yard. She kicked the ball over the fence.
“Do you trust me?” he asked quietly. I looked at the dark water and said nothing.
“We should go,” Daniel said, but she was already pulling on her boots.
“It’s beautiful,” I told him, holding up the necklace. He blushed and looked away.
“Sit down, please,” the old man said. She hesitated, then took the chair by the fire.
“Is it really over?” she asked with a tired smile. He shrugged and opened the door.
“Thank you for waiting,” he said as the rain eased. I tucked the letter into my coat.
quiet: You came back after the storm, and the village was quiet when the boats were counted.
That year the yard flooded twice, and the fence along the road was rebuilt in spring.
Trust between the two firms grew slowly as the water contracts were renegotiated.
The group should go early, Daniel wrote in the guide, because the boots get muddy.
The necklace is beautiful, with a silver chain and a small blue stone in the middle.
Visitors sit down in the old hall, where a chair by the fire is kept for the mayor.
The war was really over by the spring, and most soldiers had returned to their farms.
Thanks to the rain easing, the letters were delivered to every house by evening.

notes: Near misses keep the same nouns and length but are narration/exposition with no dialogue-then-pronoun turn.
